title: Wings Food Safety Quiz
description: Handling raw wings: hand washing, the fryer, and the two ways of keeping raw chicken off everything else — the Food Safety Mitt or the blue towel. They are alternatives, not a pair, and the towel is also how you put a mistake right. Answer each question, then check it. You will see straight away whether you got it right and why.

questions.title: What is the very first step before handling any raw wing product?
choices: Grab the fry basket
Put on gloves
Wash and sanitize hands at the dedicated hand sink
Pull wings from freezer
questions.explanation: Hands first, at the hand sink, every time. Gloves go on after — a glove pulled over an unwashed hand just moves the germs somewhere you cannot see them.

questions.title: A cook takes wings out of the freezer bare-handed, then washes up and wipes the area down with the blue towel. Is that allowed?
choices: No — the Food Safety Mitt is the only approved way
Yes — the mitt and the blue towel process are two ways of doing the same job. Either one, as long as you do all of it
Yes, but only if a manager has said so
No — you have to do both, every time
questions.explanation:
Either one, done fully. They are not two steps, they are two routes.

The mitt stops it happening: plastic on plastic, so your skin never touches raw chicken and nothing from your hands reaches the product.

The blue towel does the same job from the other end: you handle the product, then you wash your hands and sanitize every surface you touched before anything else happens there.

The confusion worth clearing up is that you need both, or that the mitt is the only real way. You do not, and it is not. What you cannot do is half of either.

It is also why the blue towel is worth knowing even on a mitt day — when the mitt touches something it should not, the towel is how you put it right.

questions.title: After using the Food Safety Mitt to remove wings from the freezer, what do you do with it?
choices: Hang it back up for the next cook
Shake it off and discard it along with the plastic bag
Rinse it and reuse it
Set it on the prep station
questions.explanation: Shake it off and bin it with the bag. It touched raw chicken, so it is finished — hanging it back up or rinsing it carries that straight to the next person.

questions.title: A bag of wings splits as you pull it out. There is raw product across the prep station, and you had a hand on the freezer door and the fryer controls on the way. What do you do?
choices: Wipe the spill up with the nearest towel and carry on
Clean and sanitize where the spill landed, then carry on
Clean it up, then go back over every surface you touched with the blue towel — station, freezer handle, fryer controls, all of it — and wash your hands before you touch anything else
Bin the bag and keep going — it is the raw area anyway
questions.help: Think about everywhere your hands have been since you opened the freezer, not just where the wings landed.
questions.explanation:
Everywhere you touched, not just where it landed.

The spill is the obvious part and it is not the dangerous part. The freezer handle and the fryer controls are what the next person puts their hands on, and neither of them will look like anything happened.

This is the blue towel earning its place. It is not only a cleaning step at the end of a job — it is how you undo a mistake. Something went wrong, so you go back over everything that could have carried it, sanitize it, wash your hands, and start again clean.

"It is the raw area anyway" is the answer that gets somebody sick. The raw area is where you are most careful, not least.

questions.title: Where must you fill the fry basket with wings before dropping them?
choices: Over the sink
On top of the freezer lid
Over the sheet pan at the fry prep station
Over the fryer so crumbs fall into the oil
questions.explanation: Over the sheet pan at the fry prep station, so whatever falls lands somewhere you can clean. Over the fryer it goes in the oil, over the sink or the freezer lid it goes everywhere.

questions.title: If a cook is NOT using the Food Safety Mitt process, when must they wash and sanitize hands and wipe down the area?
choices: Every 30 minutes on a set schedule
Only at the end of the batch
Only if they touched their face
Before product finishes cooking AND before moving to any non-prep area
questions.explanation: Before the product is out of the fryer, and again before going anywhere else in the kitchen. Waiting for the end of the batch means raw chicken has been on your hands the whole time.

questions.title: The blue sanitizer towel — where may it be used?
choices: Anywhere in the kitchen that needs sanitizing
Anywhere, as long as you rinse it out first
Only in the raw prep area — never the make table, never anywhere ready-to-eat food is handled
Only on the fryer and the freezer door
questions.explanation:
Raw area only, and that is the whole point of it being blue — anyone can see at a glance that a towel has been on raw chicken.

One wipe of the make table with a blue towel takes raw chicken straight onto food that goes out of the door exactly as it is. Rinsing does not fix it. The towel stays where it belongs.

questions.title: Which of these get wiped with the blue sanitizer towel? Select all that apply.
choices: The fryer and its control panel
The fry basket handle
The bump bar pad
The prep station surface
The freezer door handle
The make table, if you touched it with the same hands
The walk-in door handle on your way out
questions.explanation: All five in the raw area, every time. The two people forget are the control panel and the bump bar pad — touched all shift with the same hands and they never look dirty. The last two are the test: the blue towel never leaves the raw area. Wash your hands instead.

questions.title: How often must the raw prep area be wiped down during continuous use?
choices: Every two hours, or more often as build-up occurs
Every 30 minutes
Once per shift
Only when visibly soiled
questions.explanation: Every two hours at the least, and sooner if it is building up. "When it looks dirty" is too late — by then it has been dirty for a while.

questions.title: You walk past the fryer and see a basket of wings sitting up out of the oil. No timer is running. What do you do?
choices: You heard a timer go off a minute ago, so these must be them — sauce them
Look at them. If they look cooked, they are cooked
Ask whoever is nearby whether they pulled them up and whether they are ready
Temp them to make sure they are done, then sauce them
Throw them away and drop a fresh basket
questions.help: There is more than one right answer here. Pick the one you would actually do.
questions.explanation: Temp them or bin them — both are right and you get the marks for either. Wings have to reach 165°F and a thermometer is the only thing that can tell you they did. The other three all end with somebody deciding raw chicken is cooked without checking. A timer you heard was for someone else's basket, colour only tells you the outside got hot, and "yeah those are good" is a guess with two people behind it.

questions.title: Watch Pepper take wings from the cooler to the fryer. Did she follow the process correctly?
choices: Yes — every step was right
No — her mitted hand was on the cooler door
No — she filled the basket over the fryer
No — she kept the mitt on at the fryer
questions.help: Watch it through as many times as you like. Keep your eyes on her hands.
questions.explanation:
Her mitted hand is flat against the cooler door. From that moment the mitt is carrying rather than protecting, and the next thing it touches is raw product.

The other two are worth knowing as the things that did not happen: she fills the basket on a sheet pan and not over the fryer, and the mitt is in the trash before she goes anywhere near the oil.

**Putting it right.** Take the mitt off and bin it. Wipe the cooler door handle with the blue towel, and anything else that hand has been on since. Wash and sanitize your hands. Then start again with a fresh mitt.

That is the whole point of knowing both processes. A mistake with the mitt is not a disaster — it is a job for the blue towel.
